log.text: Folded CBS Challenge Map v2 (post-11 Jun alignment) into the board: 9 challenges (C1–C9) as watch/disc items + 2 levers (L1–L2) as actions. Critical reinforcing loop: C1 (liability) ↔ C5 (identity) — seeking liability protection triggers staff-aug reclassification. Suggested sequence: C5 → C1 → C4 → C2 → C7 → C3 → C8 → C9 → C6. Levers to test: L1 ring-fencing (Adrian Scales' proposal), L2 land-and-expand reframe (Jake). Source: EoD_Challenge_Map_v2.html (CBS working artefact).

items.title: C1 — Legal / liability friction blocks onboarding
items.detail: Critical · impact 92 · addressability 28 · linked: C2, C4. — Reconfirmed as the crux. The block is the indemnity clause more than the commercials: Exxon wants unlimited liability on a ~£350K contract; a £10M cap still stalls it. Critically, the pass-through partner does NOT solve it — Raise inherits and flows down the same terms. Negotiating protection also creates visibility that triggers staff-aug reclassification (see loop to C5). — Decision it forces: Is there any pragmatic liability route that survives a supermajor — partner, ring-fenced entity, or a capped position they will accept — or is new-logo growth structurally blocked?

items.title: C2 — The promise outruns the delivery
items.detail: Critical · impact 84 · addressability 50 · linked: C1, C5, C7. — Confirmed and concrete: the six-week speed promise to Exxon broke, one vetted candidate lost outright, a second walked, ~£4K sunk on sourcing for an unclosable deal. Proposed reframe on the table: stop selling first-engagement speed, sell post-onboarding long-term agility instead. — Decision it forces: Do we re-cut the value prop to "slow to start, then fast forever", or narrow the promise to what we can reliably deliver today?

items.title: C3 — The moat doesn't travel
items.detail: Critical · impact 80 · addressability 24 · linked: C9, C4, C8, C6. — Confirmed. Wins rest on reputation — originally NAG's product reputation, now the emerging HPC/BP reputation — plus relationships. Reputation travels weakly to new logos; relationships not at all. Decays fast outside BP and O&G. — Decision it forces: Is there a portable asset — a productised model, a bench, a partner network — that can win without one person's relationships?

items.title: C4 — No engine beneath the MD
items.detail: Critical · impact 86 · addressability 76 · linked: C1, C3, C6. — No talent bench, no technical recruiters, no documented operations; every account leans on James. The £4K-of-LinkedIn, candidates-lost episode is this gap in action. Still the one high-impact challenge squarely within our control — and it unlocks several others. — Decision it forces: What repeatable engine — sourcing bench, recruiting capacity, an account-leadership layer — removes the single-person dependency and lets a fourth account stand up without grinding James down?

items.title: C5 — Identity — and it's being decided for us
items.detail: Critical · impact 88 · addressability 42 · linked: C2, C7, C8. — Hardened. You said it plainly: we are functionally staff aug with extras that justify margin. The new edge: Exxon procurement is imposing the staff-aug classification regardless of how we frame the SOW, dragging us toward competing with commodity staffing firms. Identity is no longer purely our choice. — Decision it forces: Do we deliberately own a specialist HPC/AI staff-aug identity, fight to be classified as services, or split the two by route?

items.title: C6 — Fractional bench blocked by IP
items.detail: Opportunity · impact 64 · addressability 33 · linked: C4, C3. — Total (Keith Gray) and BP (Elizabeth Althow) are pulling for a shared fractional / project bench. Blocked by competitor-confidentiality; the CCA vehicle exists but is heavyweight. Died once under cold outreach — relationships have since warmed. — Decision it forces: Is the consortium / fractional model worth the legal weight now, or parked until the engine and relationships are stronger?

items.title: C7 — Cross-sell never operationalised
items.detail: Opportunity · impact 70 · addressability 80 · linked: C2, C5. — Group expertise is sold but never delivered into accounts. Total's Donnie Cooper has explicitly asked for the differentiation versus StaffHawk; year-end conversion is the prize. Warm, fast, within control. — Decision it forces: Can we land one real cross-sell engagement into an existing account this quarter to prove the services story is more than a pitch?

items.title: C8 — Attribution — largely answered
items.detail: Foundational · impact 54 · addressability 72 · linked: C5, C3. — The alignment call effectively settled this: every win (BP extensions, Total, Exxon) was opportunistic inbound to a known provider on reputation — clients are not buying into a value prop. The question is now answered, but the answer is that there is no controllable acquisition engine yet. — Decision it forces: Given growth has been reputation-driven inbound, can that be deliberately engineered — or only protected?

items.title: C9 — BP concentration + catastrophic-risk exposure
items.detail: Foundational · impact 80 · addressability 28 · linked: C3. — Now has a concrete vector: an unlimited-indemnity signature on a small contract could sink the group. And the anchor is softening — BP forecast down £4.93M → £4.5M, staff being moved to India (defence question parked), prior cost-cutting. Bounds the risk appetite hard. — Decision it forces: What is the most growth we can pursue without ever putting BP — or the group balance sheet via indemnity — at risk?

items.title: L1 — Liability ring-fencing (separate EoD entity)
items.detail: Lever · potential 60 · feasibility 40 · acts on: C1, C9. — Adrian Scales' proposal: a standalone EoD subsidiary to contain liability so a worst case can't bleed into the group. Partial mitigation for C1 and C9 — but counterparties will likely demand an affiliate/parent-guarantee clause and defeat it. Worth scoping, not banking on. — Open question: Would a ring-fenced entity hold up against a supermajor's affiliate clause, and is the legal cost justified by the protection it actually delivers?

items.title: L2 — Land-and-expand reframe (Jake)
items.detail: Lever · potential 66 · feasibility 55 · acts on: C1, C2. — Jake's challenge: if the model is one client a year grown from ~$100K to several $M, the onboarding/liability friction is a one-time entry cost and the speed shows up later as agility. Total reportedly framed SC as a long-term partnership. If true, it splits C1 — a barrier to new logos, not to expanding landed accounts. Untested against the opportunistic-inbound pattern. — Open question: Is there real evidence a client will buy the long-term-agility vision and expand — or is every deal a discrete project that ends?
